KEKERASAI.I

CHAPTER I

GENERAL PROVISIONS

Article 1

In this Regional Regulation, what is meant by: 1. Regency is Musi Rawas Regency; 2. Regency Government is the Government of Musi Rawas Regency; 4
3. Regent is the Regent of Musi Rawas. 4. Domestic Violence is any act against a person, especially women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or deprivation of liberty unlawfully within the scope of the household. 5. Elimination of Domestic Violence is a guarantee provided by the state to prevent the occurrence of domestic violence, prosecute perpetrators of domestic violence, and protect victims of domestic violence. 6. Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payment or benefits, so as to obtain the consent of the person holding control over that other person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in the person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, caused by the criminal act of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or may result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that causes pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, unconsciousness and/or causes death
10. Psychological violence is an act that causes fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Sexual violence is an act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, forced unnatural or unwanted sexual intercourse, forced sexual intercourse with others for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes. 12. Victim is a woman and child who experiences misery and/or suffering either directly or indirectly as a result of violence. 13. Women in contact with the law are women in conflict with the law, women as victims, women as witnesses or women as parties. 14. Child is a person under the age of 18 years, including those in the womb. 15. Family is the smallest unit in society consisting of husband and wife, or husband and wife and their children, or father and his children, or mother and her children, or blood relatives in direct lineage upward or downward up to the third degree. 16. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or step father and/or mother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 17. Guardian is a person or body that in reality exercises custodial power as a parent over a child. 18. Neglected child is a child whose needs are not properly fulfilled, whether physical, mental, spiritual, or social. 19. Child with Disability is a child who experiences physical and/or mental impairment so as to interfere with his/her growth and development properly. 20. Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of the authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of that child, into the family environment of the adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child who is cared for by a person or institution, to be given guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because his/her parents or one of his/her parents is unable to guarantee the child's proper growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, foster, protect, and develop the child in accordance with the religion professed and the ability, talent, and interest. 24. Rights of the child are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, community, government, and the state. 25. Protection is all efforts aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecutors, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so that they can live, grow, develop, and participate, optimally in accordance with human dignity and dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Special protection is protection given to children in emergency situations, children in conflict with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children who are exploited economically and/or sexually, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substance abuse (napza), children who are victims of kidnapping, sale, trafficking, children who are victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children who are victims of abuse and neglect. 28. Service is an action taken as soon as possible to the victim when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against the victim will, is, or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to empower victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of Recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims to conduct counseling, therapy and advocacy for the empowerment and recovery of victims of violence. 33.

Article 81 states: (1) Every person who intentionally commits violence or threat of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to every person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the sentence shall be increased by 1/3 (one third) of the sentence as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Every person who intentionally commits violence or threat of violence, coercion, fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the sentence shall be increased by 1/3 (one third) of the sentence as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for themselves or for sale, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of at most Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the heaviest criminal threat is Article 295, namely 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law has been quite severe in establishing criminal and fine threats as regulated in Article 81 to Article 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established heavy threats or legal sanctions, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally implemented them, so there is still a gap between law in books and law in action. In cases as regulated in Article 81 to Article 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigation and inquiry processes that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in prosecution and judges' verdicts they are still light so they are not in accordance with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household scope, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays domestic violence is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of domestic violence in Musi Rawas Regency, the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency has established an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/KPTS/KPP/2015, namely concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) serves as a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is domestic violence or other violence affecting women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, however the existence of P2TP2A is not yet widely known by the community. Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, in essence is to realize a household that is sakinah, mawadah, and warohmah, this can be read from the objectives of eliminating domestic violence, namely: (a) preventing all forms of domestic violence (KDRT); (b) protecting victims of domestic violence, (c) taking action against perpetrators of domestic violence and (d) maintaining the integrity of a harmonious and prosperous household. So that we better understand the prohibition of domestic violence, the important matters of Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning domestic violence will be briefly described as follows: Types of domestic violence, include:
a. physical violence, is an act that results in (1) pain, (2) falling ill, or (3) serious injury; b. psychological violence, is an act that results in (1) fear, (2) loss of self-confidence, (3) loss of ability to act, (4) feeling of helplessness, (5) and/or severe psychological suffering to a person; c. sexual violence includes: (1) forced sexual relations committed against a person including a child, residing within the household scope, (2) forced sexual relations against one person within the household scope with another person including a child, for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes; d. household neglect, includes (1) neglecting a person including a child within the household scope, whereas according to the law applicable to them or because of an agreement or contract they are obliged to provide livelihood, care, or maintenance to that person or child, (2) resulting in economic dependence by limiting and/or prohibiting proper work inside or outside the home so that the victim is under the control of that person. The rights of domestic violence victims are to receive: (1) protection from family, police, prosecution, court, advocates, social institutions, or other parties either temporarily or based on a court order; (2) health services in accordance with medical needs; (3) special handling related to victim confidentiality; 4.

Article 2

Letter a Sufficiently clear. Letter b Justice, gender equality, this principle is very important because in reality there are still many victims who have not received justice, let alone recovery and reintegration, which are the rights of victims of violence in accordance with the provisions of laws and regulations, including Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, and Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning the Eradication of the Crime of Trafficking in Persons. If this principle is not guaranteed and not implemented, then victims will become marginalized parties, so that it can cause incidents that we do not expect, for example becoming mentally ill and even to the desire and implementation of the desire to commit suicide because they no longer have hope of being accepted by society, even by their own family. Many experiences like this have occurred in the Indonesian nation, let us end this humanitarian tragedy, because we recognize that even though they are victims and even perpetrators of violence, they remain Indonesian citizens, who have the right to Human Rights that we jointly proclaim to be respected and implemented. Amen Letter c Non-discrimination, we often do not realize that we do this principle, for example differences in ethnicity, race, gender, religion, marital status, social status and many more. The principle of non-discrimination requires us to treat ourselves and others equally, equitably, fairly as ordinary human beings.

Letter d Best interests of victims, is a principle specific to women that can only be formulated by the woman herself. Female victims of violence want to be given freedom in accordance with their interests, women want to forget the perpetrator who is actually a person they once loved, and so on. So we as a society or as law enforcement officials need to give women the opportunity to express their interests regarding everything related to the perpetrator and how to overcome the impact of the violence that befalls them.

Article 40

Special protection for child victims of violence as referred to in Article 30 includes: physical, psychological, and sexual violence shall be carried out through efforts: dissemination and socialization of provisions of laws and regulations that protect child victims of violence; and monitoring, reporting, and imposition of sanctions.

Every person is prohibited from placing, allowing, committing, ordering the commission of, or participating in violence as referred to in paragraph (1).

REGIONAL REGULATION OF MUSI RAWAS REGENCY

NUMBER T. YEAR 2017

CONCERNING

PROTECTION OF WOMEN AND CHILDREN VICTIMS OF VIOLENCE

GENERAL

I. The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) eternal peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the formulator of laws and regulations and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The State of the Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtsstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it.

Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), not only to express local wisdom, but also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Criminal Act of Trafficking in Persons, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Supreme Court Regulation Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women in Contact with the Law. The principles of this Regional Regulation are principles contained in previous laws and regulations, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, are actually already contained in

Article 41

Special protection for children with disabilities as referred to in Article 30 shall be carried out through efforts:
a. treatment of children in a humane manner in accordance with the dignity and rights of the child;
b. fulfillment of special needs; andc. obtaining equal treatment with other children to achieve full social integration and individual development as much as possible.

Every person is prohibited from treating children by disregarding their views in a discriminatory manner, including labeling and equalization in education for children with disabilities.

Article 42 Special protection for child victims of abuse and neglect as referred to in Article 30 shall be carried out through supervision, prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation by the government and society.

Every person is prohibited from placing, allowing, involving, ordering the involvement of children in situations of abuse and neglect as referred to in paragraph (1).

Article 27

The 1945 Constitution, which essentially constitutes legal provisions on gender equality and justice, while also reflecting the recognition of Human Rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen naturally consists of men and women, having equal standing in the field of law and government.

Also in Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially stipulates that every person, naturally both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the rights of citizens to obtain facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, naturally including women and children victims of violence.

Violence whose victims are women and children occurs both within marriage and outside marriage. Whereas Law Number 1 of 1974 concerning Marriage, which in Article 1 regulates the definition of marriage as a physical and spiritual bond between a man and a woman to build a household based on the One Supreme God. Article 30 stipulates that the obligation of husband and wife is to be faithful to each other, love, and help.

In this Marriage Law, it is regulated regarding who becomes a biological child, as well as joint property, including the method of continuing its ownership or inheritance to the children. If this Law is complied with, it can prevent and eliminate Domestic Violence, unfortunately what happens in society is that Domestic Violence (KDRT) is increasingly rampant, precisely with modus operandi that are increasingly complex and cause increasingly horrifying consequences. The principle of non-discrimination is in line with the recognition of Human Rights, therefore it is very appropriate that the Government of Indonesia by enacting Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), in Article 1 states the definition of discrimination against women and all its consequences if discrimination against women occurs.

Basically working is only for adults, while children, namely people aged under 18 years, are obliged to study and play. However, due to family economic limitations, there are some children who must work. Therefore Law Number 20 of 1999, concerning the Minimum Age Limit for Children to be able to work by providing provisions that parents and employers should pay attention to the provisions of this Law, so that even though children are forced to work, they do not lose their youth and can still attend school to guarantee their future. Children who are forced to work are found in all areas, both in urban and rural areas. In order for children to obtain their rights, the socialization of Law Number 20 of 1999 is urgent to be carried out.

As a consequence of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia as a State that signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights is the answer. Considering that although since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of Human Rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which clearly constitutes a violation of Human Rights. In Law Number 39 of 1999 it is reaffirmed that women's rights are Human Rights (Article 45) and Article 52 paragraph (2), which states that Children's rights are Human Rights and for the benefit of children's rights they are recognized and protected by law even from the womb.

This means that children are recognized as having freedom and liberty in accordance with their dignity as human beings, so that any form of violence whatsoever must not occur to children, because it constitutes a violation of Human Rights.

The commitment and political will of the Government of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia to protect children is reinforced by the enactment of Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection. In accordance with the types of crimes against children which are increasingly occurring today, we need to study the provisions of articles 77 to 90, which already provide sufficiently severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this regional regulation for cases occurring in society are those violating Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice

Article 4

The purpose of establishing this Regional Regulation is to provide protection and services to women and children victims of violence based on gender and the best interests of the child occurring in the household and/or public sphere, as well as to guarantee the fulfillment of children's rights so they can live, grow, develop, and participate optimally in accordance with human dignity and honor, and receive protection from violence and discrimination, for the realization of Indonesian children who are of quality, noble character, and prosperous.

Assistance is all actions in the form of counseling, psychological therapy, advocacy, and spiritual guidance, for the empowerment of victims of domestic violence to resolve the problems faced. 34. Integrated Service Center for the Empowerment of Women and Children (P2TP2A) hereinafter abbreviated as P2TP2A is an institution providing services to victims of violence, based in hospitals, managed jointly in the form of medical services (including medico-legal), psycho-social and legal services. 35. Cooperation is a systematic and integrated manner among recovery implementers in providing services to recover victims of domestic violence. 36. Safe house is a temporary residence used to provide protection to victims in accordance with established operational standards. 37. Community is individuals, families, groups, and social organizations and/or community organizations. 38. Every person is an individual or corporation. 39. Household is family members, relatives (grandchildren, nieces/nephews, older siblings, younger siblings, grandfathers, grandmothers, cousins and so on) and non-relatives (servants, drivers and so on) who live and eat from one kitchen and reside in one house.

Article6l Any person who intentionally does not provide protection to women and children such that:
a. causes violence to occur;
b. allows violence to occur; and/orc. does not report and does not provide protection to victims, shall be subject to sanctions in accordance with the provisions of legislation.

Article 37

1. Special protection for children who are exploited economically and/or sexually as referred to in Article 30 is the obligation and responsibility of the government and society.
2. Special protection for children who are exploited as referred to in paragraph (1) shall be carried out through:a. Dissemination and/or socialization of provisions of laws and regulations related to the protection of children who are exploited economically and/or sexually;
b. monitoring, reporting, and imposition of sanctions; andc. involvement of various government agencies, companies, labor unions, non-governmental organizations, and the community in the elimination of economic and/or sexual exploitation of children.
3. Every person is prohibited from placing, allowing, committing, ordering the commission of, or participating in the exploitation of children as referred to in paragraph (1).

CHAPTER II

VICTIMS' RIGHTS

Article 5

Every woman and child victim of violence has the right to obtain a. protection from family, police, prosecutors, courts, advocates, social institutions, or other parties either temporarily or based on a protection order from the court; b. health services in accordance with medical needs;
c. special handling related to victim confidentiality; d. assistance by social workers and legal aid at every level of the examination process in accordance with the provisions of laws and regulations; and e. spiritual guidance services

CHAPTER III

OBLIGATIONS AND RESPONSIBILITIES

Article 6

The District Government and the District community are obliged and responsible to carry out efforts to prevent the occurrence of violence, in the form of:

Article 10

1. For the implementation of protection for women and children, the District Government is obliged to provide services for victims in the form of: a. establishing and facilitating the implementation of integrated service institutions for victims involving community elements; and b. encouraging community awareness of the importance of protection for victims.
2. . The District Government in carrying out the obligations as referred to in paragraph (1), must pay attention to the rights and obligations of parents, guardians, husbands or other persons legally responsible for victims.
3. . The implementation of the Protection Institution for victims is carried out in an integrated manner within the P.ZTP2,A- framework (4) Further provisions regarding P2IflP2,A are regulated in a Regent Regulation.

I. The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) eternal peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the formulator of laws and regulations and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The State of the Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtsstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it.

Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), not only to express local wisdom, but also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

GENERAL

I. The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) eternal peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the formulator of laws and regulations and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The State of the Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtsstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it.

Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), not only to express local wisdom, but also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

Domestic Violence is any act against a person, especially women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or deprivation of liberty unlawfully within the scope of the household. 5. Elimination of Domestic Violence is a guarantee provided by the state to prevent the occurrence of domestic violence, prosecute perpetrators of domestic violence, and protect victims of domestic violence. 6. Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payment or benefits, so as to obtain the consent of the person holding control over that other person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in the person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, caused by the criminal act of trafficking in persons. 8. 10. Psychological violence is an act that causes fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household scope, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays domestic violence is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of domestic violence in Musi Rawas Regency, the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency has established an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/KPTS/KPP/2015, namely concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) serves as a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is domestic violence or other violence affecting women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, however the existence of P2TP2A is not yet widely known by the community. Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, in essence is to realize a household that is sakinah, mawadah, and warohmah, this can be read from the objectives of eliminating domestic violence, namely: (a) preventing all forms of domestic violence (KDRT); (b) protecting victims of domestic violence, (c) taking action against perpetrators of domestic violence and (d) maintaining the integrity of a harmonious and prosperous household. So that we better understand the prohibition of domestic violence, the important matters of Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning domestic violence will be briefly described as follows: Types of domestic violence, include:
a. physical violence, is an act that results in (1) pain, (2) falling ill, or (3) serious injury; b. psychological violence, is an act that results in (1) fear, (2) loss of self-confidence, (3) loss of ability to act, (4) feeling of helplessness, (5) and/or severe psychological suffering to a person; c. sexual violence includes: (1) forced sexual relations committed against a person including a child, residing within the household scope, (2) forced sexual relations against one person within the household scope with another person including a child, for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes; d. household neglect, includes (1) neglecting a person including a child within the household scope, whereas according to the law applicable to them or because of an agreement or contract they are obliged to provide livelihood, care, or maintenance to that person or child, (2) resulting in economic dependence by limiting and/or prohibiting proper work inside or outside the home so that the victim is under the control of that person. The rights of domestic violence victims are to receive: (1) protection from family, police, prosecution, court, advocates, social institutions, or other parties either temporarily or based on a court order; (2) health services in accordance with medical needs; (3) special handling related to victim confidentiality; 4.

Safe house is a temporary residence used to provide protection to victims in accordance with established operational standards. 37. Community is individuals, families, groups, and social organizations and/or community organizations. 38. Every person is an individual or corporation. 39. Household is family members, relatives (grandchildren, nieces/nephews, older siblings, younger siblings, grandfathers, grandmothers, cousins and so on) and non-relatives (servants, drivers and so on) who live and eat from one kitchen and reside in one house.

Article 81 states: (1) Every person who intentionally commits violence or threat of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to every person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the sentence shall be increased by 1/3 (one third) of the sentence as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Every person who intentionally commits violence or threat of violence, coercion, fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the sentence shall be increased by 1/3 (one third) of the sentence as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for themselves or for sale, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of at most Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the heaviest criminal threat is Article 295, namely 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law has been quite severe in establishing criminal and fine threats as regulated in Article 81 to Article 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established heavy threats or legal sanctions, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally implemented them, so there is still a gap between law in books and law in action. In cases as regulated in Article 81 to Article 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigation and inquiry processes that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in prosecution and judges' verdicts they are still light so they are not in accordance with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household scope, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays domestic violence is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of domestic violence in Musi Rawas Regency, the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency has established an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/KPTS/KPP/2015, namely concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) serves as a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is domestic violence or other violence affecting women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, however the existence of P2TP2A is not yet widely known by the community. Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, in essence is to realize a household that is sakinah, mawadah, and warohmah, this can be read from the objectives of eliminating domestic violence, namely: (a) preventing all forms of domestic violence (KDRT); (b) protecting victims of domestic violence, (c) taking action against perpetrators of domestic violence and (d) maintaining the integrity of a harmonious and prosperous household. So that we better understand the prohibition of domestic violence, the important matters of Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning domestic violence will be briefly described as follows: Types of domestic violence, include:
a. physical violence, is an act that results in (1) pain, (2) falling ill, or (3) serious injury; b. psychological violence, is an act that results in (1) fear, (2) loss of self-confidence, (3) loss of ability to act, (4) feeling of helplessness, (5) and/or severe psychological suffering to a person; c. sexual violence includes: (1) forced sexual relations committed against a person including a child, residing within the household scope, (2) forced sexual relations against one person within the household scope with another person including a child, for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes; d. household neglect, includes (1) neglecting a person including a child within the household scope, whereas according to the law applicable to them or because of an agreement or contract they are obliged to provide livelihood, care, or maintenance to that person or child, (2) resulting in economic dependence by limiting and/or prohibiting proper work inside or outside the home so that the victim is under the control of that person. The rights of domestic violence victims are to receive: (1) protection from family, police, prosecution, court, advocates, social institutions, or other parties either temporarily or based on a court order; (2) health services in accordance with medical needs; (3) special handling related to victim confidentiality; 4.

Assistance is all actions in the form of counseling, psychological therapy, advocacy, and spiritual guidance, for the empowerment of victims of domestic violence to resolve the problems faced. 34. Cooperation is a systematic and integrated manner among recovery implementers in providing services to recover victims of domestic violence. 36. So that we better understand the prohibition of domestic violence, the important matters of Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning domestic violence will be briefly described as follows: Types of domestic violence, include:
a. physical violence, is an act that results in (1) pain, (2) falling ill, or (3) serious injury; b. psychological violence, is an act that results in (1) fear, (2) loss of self-confidence, (3) loss of ability to act, (4) feeling of helplessness, (5) and/or severe psychological suffering to a person; c. sexual violence includes: (1) forced sexual relations committed against a person including a child, residing within the household scope, (2) forced sexual relations against one person within the household scope with another person including a child, for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes; d. household neglect, includes (1) neglecting a person including a child within the household scope, whereas according to the law applicable to them or because of an agreement or contract they are obliged to provide livelihood, care, or maintenance to that person or child, (2) resulting in economic dependence by limiting and/or prohibiting proper work inside or outside the home so that the victim is under the control of that person. The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) eternal peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the formulator of laws and regulations and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The State of the Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtsstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it.

Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), not only to express local wisdom, but also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

REGIONAL REGULATION OF MUSI RAWAS REGENCY

NUMBER T. YEAR 2017

CONCERNING

PROTECTION OF WOMEN AND CHILDREN VICTIMS OF VIOLENCE

GENERAL

I. The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) eternal peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the formulator of laws and regulations and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The State of the Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtsstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, in essence is to realize a household that is sakinah, mawadah, and warohmah, this can be read from the objectives of eliminating domestic violence, namely: (a) preventing all forms of domestic violence (KDRT); (b) protecting victims of domestic violence, (c) taking action against perpetrators of domestic violence and (d) maintaining the integrity of a harmonious and prosperous household. So that we better understand the prohibition of domestic violence, the important matters of Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning domestic violence will be briefly described as follows: Types of domestic violence, include:

Article 82 states: (1) Every person who intentionally commits violence or threat of violence, coercion, fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the heaviest criminal threat is Article 295, namely 12 years. The problem is, even though the Law has established heavy threats or legal sanctions, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally implemented them, so there is still a gap between law in books and law in action. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household scope, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays domestic violence is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of domestic violence in Musi Rawas Regency, the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency has established an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/KPTS/KPP/2015, namely concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) serves as a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is domestic violence or other violence affecting women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, however the existence of P2TP2A is not yet widely known by the community. Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, in essence is to realize a household that is sakinah, mawadah, and warohmah, this can be read from the objectives of eliminating domestic violence, namely: (a) preventing all forms of domestic violence (KDRT); (b) protecting victims of domestic violence, (c) taking action against perpetrators of domestic violence and (d) maintaining the integrity of a harmonious and prosperous household. So that we better understand the prohibition of domestic violence, the important matters of Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning domestic violence will be briefly described as follows: Types of domestic violence, include:
a. physical violence, is an act that results in (1) pain, (2) falling ill, or (3) serious injury; b. psychological violence, is an act that results in (1) fear, (2) loss of self-confidence, (3) loss of ability to act, (4) feeling of helplessness, (5) and/or severe psychological suffering to a person; c. sexual violence includes: (1) forced sexual relations committed against a person including a child, residing within the household scope, (2) forced sexual relations against one person within the household scope with another person including a child, for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes; d. household neglect, includes (1) neglecting a person including a child within the household scope, whereas according to the law applicable to them or because of an agreement or contract they are obliged to provide livelihood, care, or maintenance to that person or child, (2) resulting in economic dependence by limiting and/or prohibiting proper work inside or outside the home so that the victim is under the control of that person. Domestic Violence is any act against a person, especially women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or deprivation of liberty unlawfully within the scope of the household. 5. 10. Psychological violence is an act that causes fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11.
